JudgeSense (Bellibatlu, Raff and Zhang 2026, arXiv 2604.23478 v3): rewording a judge's instruction while keeping its question moves graded verdicts beyond repeat noise (pooled coherence −0.181), direction unstated. Khullar, Hopkins, Wang and Roger 2026 (arXiv 2603.04582; Claude 3.5 Haiku, Sonnet 4, Opus 4.1): explicit authorship statements move leniency within 0.5 of 10, i.e. up to 5 of 100, above both bars here, and they concern authorship, not a lead-in, so they bound S loosely and do not predict a miss. Grossmann and Kross 2014 (Psychological Science 25:1571): a third-person, distancing wording shrank a human self-other gap; an analogy only, since neither closing line refers to the self. Fox, Caspy and Reisler 1994 (found by the design review's search; abstract only): a cautionary instruction did not reduce human self-rating leniency, while changes to the rating scale and form did. What this bet adds over Chen: the first closing-line-only swap on a graded penalty for a planted overclaim, in a quoted User/Assistant transcript of the model's own conversation, on Claude 5.5 models, with both lines graded in one run. fields.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. Papers in print already show, in our direction, that a model goes easier on the same text in its own assistant turn than in a user turn (Khullar, Hopkins, Wang and Roger 2026, arXiv 2603.04582 v1, strongest on-policy; Tsui 2025, arXiv 2507.02778 v3), and they show the rival this test removes: LLM judges disagree with themselves across identical runs (Haldar and Hockenmaier 2025, Rating Roulette, arXiv 2510.27106: Krippendorff's alpha 0.265 to 0.563 over three runs on MT-Bench, three open-weight judges; Norman, Rivera and Hughes 2026, arXiv 2606.19544 v1: test-retest above 0.95 alongside position bias above 0.10), and human rating separates drift within a session from "scale instability" across sessions (Quellmalz 1980, CSE Report 136, abstract only). The nearest case of a self-favouring effect shrinking under a stricter comparison is Roytburg et al. 2026 (arXiv 2601.22548 v2: "only 51% of initial findings retain statistical significance" once a judge's votes for its own wrong answers are set against its votes for outcome-matched other models' wrong answers), which changes the baseline, not the run, and reports no repeated runs. A direct search found nothing in print that re-measures a quoted-copy leniency gap with every cell graded in one run, set against the same gap read across runs. Here Haiku 5.5's gap stays above zero but is 46% of its same-run blunting, under the 6.3 bar with an interval that cannot rule the bar out (its fall from sg-b4 is split between the two cells, neither shift distinguishable from zero, so run-to-run noise is neither shown nor ruled out as the cause), while Opus 5.5's holds at about its full size (+5.0, against sg-b4's +4.0). Search: WebSearch and arXiv abs/HTML, 2026-11-05: "LLM judge self-attribution bias same run versus cross run"; "LLM-as-a-judge test-retest reliability between sessions drift"; "monitor leniency own assistant turn versus quoted transcript in user message"; "self-preference bias replication measurement artifact"; "LLM evaluation nondeterminism score shift baseline from earlier run"; "batch effects high-throughput data"; "rater drift within-session versus between-session". fields.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. That changing only the closing instruction of a self-review prompt moves the verdict a little, in either direction, and less than moving the text out of the model's own turn, is in print: Chen et al. 2026 (arXiv 2606.05976 v2, §4.4-4.5, Tables 4 and 7; Qwen2.5-72B math, n = 30) left a wrong claim in the model's own turn, swapped only the appended audit prompt, and saw explicit correction move from 16.7% to between 0.0% and 33.3%, against 70.0% with a system `<memory>` relabel. That rewording a judge's instruction while keeping its question moves graded verdicts beyond repeat noise, direction unreported, is in print for Claude judges (Bellibatlu, Raff and Zhang 2026, JudgeSense, arXiv 2604.23478 v3: coherence ΔJSS −0.206 for claude-haiku, −0.180 for claude-opus-4-7), and rewording a self-reflection prompt to verify rather than find mistakes cut false flips from 18.9% to 7.6% on Llama-3 8B (Liu et al. 2024, arXiv 2406.10400 v1). Not in print after a direct search: a swap of only "Now grade the conclusion above." for "Grade the conclusion." inside a quoted User/Assistant copy of the model's own conversation (the claim already out of its turn), scored as the penalty on a planted overclaim, on Claude 5.5 models with both lines graded in one run; ours fits Chen's picture of a small effect of either sign (Haiku +2.5 of 100 on a fragile mean, Opus +0.3), and no paper found separates such a line from the cross-run difference in the remainder it splits. No test of deictic cues ("now", "above") in a grading instruction was found, in LLM work or in survey question-wording research (nearest: Zhang, Meng and Collier 2024, arXiv 2406.17095, abstract only: models "do not have relative position awareness of the context"). Search: WebSearch and arXiv abs/HTML, 2026-11-05: LLM judge instruction wording sensitivity, prompt template grading score shift; closing or trailing instruction wording, self-evaluation of the model's own quoted response; self-critique prompt wording against a neutral instruction; deictic "above" wording, relative position in prompts; survey question wording and self-rating leniency; LLM judge run-to-run nondeterminism; self-preference framing, third-person lead-in; Chen et al. 2606.05976 v2 §4.4-4.5 and Tables 4 and 7 re-opened. row.prior_work: **Mixed, leaning to a miss.** Tsui 2025, Self-Correction Bench (arXiv 2507.02778 v3, §4.1; HTML opened 2026-11-05): appending "Wait" after the model's own erroneous output, as a continuation of its turn, cut the self-correction blind spot by 89.3% on average over 14 open-weight models; no Claude model is in its "Wait" results (Claude 3.5 Haiku and Sonnet 4 appear only in the blind-spot figures, footnote 2), and no condition puts "Wait" in a user message. That predicts a pass if the marker works wherever it sits. Chen et al. 2026 (arXiv 2606.05976 v2; HTML opened 2026-11-05, §3.1, §4.2–4.3, Tables 2 and 4): re-presenting a wrong claim as a user message with a "Wait," prefix did no better than the same user message without it (Claude Sonnet 4 math +40.0 points of correction either way; Qwen2.5-72B math +23.3 with, +26.7 without; the prefix higher in 2 of 12 model–domain cells), and the paper reads the trigger as "incidental and the carrier role primary"; prompts that left the claim in the model's own turn and changed only the audit instruction reached at most 23.3% correction against 16.7% (Table 4). That predicts a small W: here the flawed text stays in the model's own turn and only the user's request changes. Khullar et al. 2026 and Tsui 2025 put sg-b3's own-turn leniency itself in print (sg-b3's Novelty line: known). What this bet adds: "Wait" placed in the user's grading request with the text left in the model's turn, scored as a graded penalty on a planted overclaim, on the Claude 5.5 models, against same-run own and fresh cells. The engine's 12 sits on the miss side of a mixed prior: both Haiku and Opus must take away at least half their blunting, with two gates.
row.premortem: If this fails, the most likely reason is that 'Wait.' in the user's request leaves the flawed text in the model's own turn, so W on Haiku and Opus stays under half their blunting, as Chen et al. found for prompts that leave the claim in place.

fields.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. Papers in print already show, in our direction, that a model goes easier on the same text in its own assistant turn than in a user turn (Khullar, Hopkins, Wang and Roger 2026, arXiv 2603.04582 v1, strongest on-policy; Tsui 2025, arXiv 2507.02778 v3), and they show the rival this test removes: LLM judges disagree with themselves across identical runs (Haldar and Hockenmaier 2025, Rating Roulette, arXiv 2510.27106: Krippendorff's alpha 0.265 to 0.563 over three runs on MT-Bench, three open-weight judges), and human rating separates drift within a session from "scale instability" across sessions (Quellmalz 1980, CSE Report 136, abstract only). The nearest case of a self-favouring effect shrinking under a stricter comparison is Roytburg et al. 2026 (arXiv 2601.22548 v2: "only 51% of initial findings retain statistical significance" once a judge's votes for its own wrong answers are set against its votes for outcome-matched other models' wrong answers), which changes the baseline, not the run, and reports no repeated runs. A direct search found nothing in print that re-measures a quoted-copy leniency gap with every cell graded in one run, set against the same gap read across runs. Here Haiku 5.5's gap stays above zero but is 46% of its same-run blunting, under the 6.3 bar with an interval that cannot rule the bar out (its fall from sg-b4 is split between the two cells, neither shift distinguishable from zero, so run-to-run noise is neither shown nor ruled out as the cause), while Opus 5.5's holds at about its full size (+5.0, against sg-b4's +4.0). Search: WebSearch and arXiv abs/HTML, 2026-11-05: "LLM judge self-attribution bias same run versus cross run"; "LLM-as-a-judge test-retest reliability between sessions drift"; "monitor leniency own assistant turn versus quoted transcript in user message"; "self-preference bias replication measurement artifact"; "LLM evaluation nondeterminism score shift baseline from earlier run"; "batch effects high-throughput data"; "rater drift within-session versus between-session". By a fresh claude-opus-5-5 Novelty session (subagent).

fields.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. Tsui (2025, arXiv 2507.02778 v3, abstract and §4.1, HTML read) appended "Wait" after the model's own erroneous output and reports it cut the self-correction blind spot by 89.3% across 14 open-source non-reasoning models, with no Claude model in its "Wait" results and no condition putting the marker in a user message; Chen et al. (2026, arXiv 2606.05976 v2, Tables 1 and 2, HTML read) found a user message "Wait, c⋆" beat the same user message without the prefix in only 2 of 12 model–domain cells and state "the trigger is incidental and the carrier role primary", but there the claim itself moved into the user turn, and no "Wait" gain in their Table 2 fell below the audit-only baseline. This test's placement, the marker at the start of the user's grading request with the flawed text left in the model's own turn, scored as a graded penalty on a planted overclaim on the Claude 5.5 models, was not found in print: Opus's near-zero change agrees with Chen et al.'s reading, while Haiku's move to more leniency points the other way from both papers. The rival reading, a user turn read as doubt, has prior work on answer flipping (Laban et al. 2023, arXiv 2311.08596, abstract only: ten LLMs flipped answers 46% of the time when challenged with "Are you sure?") and on LLM evaluators swayed by user rebuttals (Kim and Khashabi 2025, EMNLP Findings, arXiv 2509.16533, abstract only), but none found tests a bare "Wait." in a grading request. Search: WebSearch plus arXiv abs/HTML reads, 2026-11-05, on "Wait" correction marker in the user turn versus the assistant turn; "Are you sure?" answer flipping and sycophancy to user doubt; LLM judge sycophancy under user rebuttal; "Wait" or reflection cues and leniency or score inflation in LLM self-evaluation; intrinsic self-correction (Huang et al. 2024, ICLR, arXiv 2310.01798, abstract only); structured reflection in clinical diagnosis (Mamede et al., search snippets only, not cited); full HTML reads of 2507.02778 v3 and 2606.05976 v2. By a fresh claude-opus-5-5 Novelty session (subagent).
